questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between row-oriented and columnar storage?
options: Row-oriented storage can only hold numeric data; columnar storage can hold any data type
Row-oriented storage keeps all columns of one row together on disk, suited to fetching single records; columnar storage keeps all values of one column together, suited to aggregating across many rows
Columnar storage does not support SQL queries
Row-oriented storage is always stored in memory, while columnar storage is always stored on disk
questions.explain: The storage layout matches the typical access pattern: row-oriented (OLTP) databases are built for fetching or updating one full record, while columnar (OLAP) stores keep each column contiguous, so an aggregate query reads only the columns it needs.

questions.q: In the real timing comparison, querying the 2-million-row Parquet file with DuckDB took about 0.0365s while the pandas filter-loop took about 0.7426s. What two factors does the lesson attribute this gap to?
options: DuckDB used a GPU while pandas did not
The columnar file format (reading only needed columns) plus vectorized GROUP BY execution inside DuckDB, versus Python-level overhead and redundant re-scanning in the filter loop
The DuckDB query used a smaller dataset than the pandas loop
pandas does not support the AVG or SUM functions
questions.explain: DuckDB benefits from both reading a columnar format (Parquet) that skips unneeded columns and executing the GROUP BY with vectorized operations, while the Python-level loop pays per-iteration overhead and re-scans the symbol column on every filter.

questions.q: What does TimescaleDB add on top of a standard PostgreSQL database?
options: A columnar-only storage engine that removes SQL support
Automatic time-based partitioning ("hypertables") while remaining a full relational database with SQL and transactional features
A proprietary query language unrelated to SQL
In-memory-only storage with no persistence
questions.explain: TimescaleDB is a PostgreSQL extension, so it keeps full relational/SQL/transactional capability while adding automatic time-based partitioning (hypertables) optimized for time-series data -- useful when both are needed in one system.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is vectorized execution inside a query engine analogous to?
options: Running a query twice to check for errors

The same idea as NumPy's vectorized array operations from Chapter 1, applied one level down inside the engine: running one operation across a contiguous chunk of column values at once instead of looping
Compressing data before writing it to disk
Encrypting query results for security
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct parallel: just as NumPy vectorized operations replace a per-element Python loop with a whole-array operation, a columnar engine's vectorized execution runs one operation across a contiguous chunk of column values instead of processing them one at a time.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what actually justifies reaching for a dedicated time-series database (like InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, or kdb+) instead of DuckDB/Parquet?
options: Simply having a large dataset, regardless of how it's queried
Wanting to avoid writing any SQL at all
Genuinely high-frequency, continuously arriving data combined with low-latency live query requirements against data still being written -- not merely data size
Needing to store more than one column of data
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that DuckDB and Parquet handle "large" data well; the case for specialized infrastructure is driven by ingestion rate and live-query latency requirements -- continuously arriving tick data with many concurrent low-latency queries -- not dataset size alone.
